nameStory: The 'Strongly Crispate' part of this moss's name comes from the Latin word 'crispus,' meaning curled or wavy, referring to how dramatically its leaves crimp and wave when they dry out. The 'Smoothcap' name points to its relatively smooth spore capsules, which lack the hairy caps that give other mosses in this family their 'haircap' nickname.
description: Strongly Crispate Smoothcap is a medium-sized moss that forms loose patches or scattered individual plants on soil and rock surfaces. Its most striking feature is how dramatically its narrow, strap-like leaves curl and twist when dry, creating an almost tortured appearance. When moist, the leaves unfurl into neat rosettes that can reach about 1-2 inches across. This moss is quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery.

idTips.label: Extremely crinkled dry leaves
idTips.description: When dry, the leaves curl and crimp so dramatically they look almost like tiny green corkscrews or crumpled paper - much more intense than other smoothcap mosses

idTips.label: Narrow, strap-shaped leaves
idTips.description: Individual leaves are long and narrow like tiny green ribbons, with a prominent midrib running down the center that you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Loose growth pattern
idTips.description: Plants grow as scattered individuals or loose patches rather than dense mats, giving the moss a more open, airy appearance

idTips.label: Smooth spore capsules
idTips.description: When present, the cylindrical spore capsules are relatively smooth and hairless, unlike the fuzzy caps of true haircap mosses

habitat: This rare moss prefers disturbed soil along trails, road cuts, and forest edges, often growing on clay-rich or compacted earth. In New England, look for it in partially shaded spots where the soil stays moderately moist but not waterlogged. It seems to favor areas with some human disturbance rather than deep, undisturbed forest.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as bright green rosettes unfurling from winter's dried remains. This is when the contrast between old crinkled leaves and fresh new growth is most obvious.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size with lush green rosettes clearly visible. Spore capsules may be present on thin stalks rising above the leaves.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin their dramatic curling as moisture decreases. The transformation from flat rosettes to twisted spirals happens quickly with the first dry spells.
seasonality.winter: Appears almost dead with leaves extremely crinkled and brownish, but springs back to life quickly when moistened with melting snow.

funFact: This moss can go from looking completely dead - with leaves so twisted they resemble tiny brown corkscrews - to bright green and photosynthesizing within minutes of getting wet, earning it a place among nature's most dramatic resurrection artists.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other smoothcap mosses, but the extremely dramatic leaf curling when dry is the giveaway - if the dried leaves look like they've been put through a torture device, you've probably found Strongly Crispate Smoothcap. Other smoothcap mosses curl much more gently.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Strongly Crispate,' this species is actually less common than regular 'Crispate Smoothcap' in most areas, which can be confusing for beginners expecting the more dramatic name to belong to the more common species.
compareHints: Compared to other smoothcap mosses like Catherine's moss or lesser smoothcap, this species has much more extreme leaf curling when dry and tends to grow in more scattered, individual plants rather than continuous patches. The leaf crinkling is so intense it's almost comical compared to the gentle waves of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Lesser smoothcap is the smallest and most delicate of New England's smoothcap mosses, with much narrower leaves than Catherine's moss or the crispate smoothcaps.
Catherine's moss stands out from its smoothcap relatives primarily by its wavy leaf margins - lesser smoothcap has narrower, flatter leaves, while crispate smoothcap has leaves that curl differently.
Compared to Lesser Smoothcap, Crispate Smoothcap has more dramatic leaf curling and tends to grow in slightly more disturbed soils.
Wavy Starburst Moss has the most dramatically wavy leaf edges of all the smoothcap mosses in New England.
